title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context (§§XXXV–XXXVI of E410): Euler sets up the planar motion of a perfectly flexible, inextensible thread whose endpoint A may itself move. Each material point is labelled by its arc length s = AM from A, so s works as a Lagrangian (material) coordinate. The tangent angle φ, measured from the fixed axis, is now a function of two variables, φ(s,t). Euler notes that this places the problem in the 'new part of analysis' on functions of two variables, and he writes partial derivatives in his parenthesis notation (dφ/ds), (dφ/dt).

Kinematics: inextensibility gives ∂x/∂s = sin φ and ∂y/∂s = cos φ. Hence x = ∫ sin φ ds and y = ∫ cos φ ds, integrated in s at fixed t. Euler stresses that x and y are nevertheless functions of both s and t.

Dynamics: the element Mm = ds has mass Σ(s) ds, with Σ the linear density, a function of s alone. Its velocity components are ∂x/∂t and ∂y/∂t, and its accelerations are ∂²x/∂t² and ∂²y/∂t². Multiplying by the mass and dividing by 2g gives the 'forces required' to produce the motion. Here g is the height fallen by a heavy body in one second, Euler's usual unit convention, so 2g is the gravitational acceleration. In modern form, (Σ ds/2g)·∂²r/∂t² is the inertial force on the element.

On the next page (§XXXVII) Euler reverses these required forces and adds them to the actual applied forces p ds and q ds. This reduces the dynamics to an instantaneous equilibrium problem, i.e. d'Alembert's principle. That step leads to the equations of motion of the inextensible string with variable density, derived from the tangential and normal equilibrium equations obtained earlier in the paper.
errors: Minor gap: since A is not fixed, x = ∫ ds sin φ and y = ∫ ds cos φ hold only up to additive 'constants' that depend on t (the coordinates of A at time t). Euler implicitly acknowledges this by integrating only in s and referring the coordinates to a fixed point. This is not a real error.
Typographical: 'itu vt' in the print should be 'ita vt'.

ideas.what: Tangent angle and coordinates of a moving inextensible curve treated as functions of the two variables (s,t), written with parenthesis partial-derivative notation
ideas.modern_name: Lagrangian/material description of a moving inextensible string; partial derivatives
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (parenthesis notation for partial differentials, 1750s); material description in continuum mechanics generally Euler/Lagrange
ideas.where_published: Euler's integral calculus and partial-differential-equation papers; string-vibration memoirs; discussed by Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Inextensibility constraint ∂x/∂s = sin φ, ∂y/∂s = cos φ for the moving string
ideas.where_published: Earlier string/chain papers of Euler; E410 itself

ideas.what: Mass element Σ(s) ds with acceleration ∂²r/∂t²; required force = mass × acceleration / 2g
ideas.modern_name: Newton's second law for a continuum element, with Euler's gravitational unit convention
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E177, 'Découverte d'un nouveau principe de mécanique', 1750/52)
ideas.where_published: E177 and many later mechanics papers

ideas.what: Reversing the required forces to reduce motion to equilibrium (next page)
ideas.where_published: Used repeatedly by Euler; discussed by Truesdell

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard setup page: two-variable kinematics of a moving string, Newton's law per element, and d'Alembert reduction. All of it is well known and analysed in Truesdell's history of flexible and elastic bodies. Nothing new is apparent.
transcription_corrections: 'itu vt' is printed as such but should read 'ita vt' (printer's error).
Velocity and acceleration expressions are in Euler's parenthesis notation, (dx/dt), (ddx/dt²); the transcription renders these correctly.
